variants.name: Resilience4j Retry with an exponential interval function
variants.implementation_notes: Resilience4j separates the mechanism from the schedule: RetryConfig carries maxAttempts (default 3, counting the initial call as the first attempt) and an IntervalFunction, and Retry.decorateCheckedSupplier/Supplier/Callable wraps the operation. IntervalFunction.ofExponentialBackoff(initialInterval, multiplier) gives the capped growth, and jitter is added with a randomized or custom interval function; retryExceptions/ignoreExceptions and retryOnResult write the classification down, and failAfterMaxAttempts makes a never-passing result predicate visible as MaxRetriesExceededException. The decorated-supplier form remains the right choice in plain-Java services; on virtual threads the wait is cheap but still parks the virtual thread, so a scheduler-based retry is only worth it in fully reactive code (CompletionStage decoration is supported).
pitfalls: maxAttempts counts the initial call as an attempt (the default 3 means one call plus two retries), and the exponential interval function caps its pre-jitter interval at maxInterval, so a randomized schedule can exceed the number you configured.

retryOnException defaults to true for every exception, so without retryExceptions/ignoreExceptions a business exception is retried; pair the configuration with failAfterMaxAttempts when a result predicate can never pass.
A Retry instance is thread-safe and meant to be shared; creating one per call does not reset per-call state (which lives in the decorated execution) and only adds allocation.

variants.name: Spring Framework 7 core retry (RetryTemplate / @Retryable)
variants.idiom_name: RetryPolicy.builder() with delay, jitter, multiplier and maxDelay
variants.implementation_notes: Spring Framework 7 moved retry support into spring-core and spring-context, and the project that used to supply it (Spring Retry) is archived; the new policy states this pattern directly as RetryPolicy.builder().delay(...).jitter(...).multiplier(...).maxDelay(...).maxAttempts(...), executed through RetryTemplate or declared with @Retryable (including on reactive methods, whose pipeline is decorated with Reactor's retry). Choose it when the application already runs on Spring Framework 7, because the policy then lives next to the method it protects and needs no extra dependency; note that maxAttempts counts only the retries, whereas Spring Retry's attribute included the initial call.
pitfalls: maxAttempts in Spring Framework counts the retry attempts only, while Spring Retry's maxAttempts included the initial invocation - migrating code silently changes the effort.
@Retryable works through a proxy, so self-invocation inside the same bean bypasses it and the call is not retried at all.
